q: Value-based vs policy-based RL?
short: Value-based learns Q and acts greedily (implicit policy); policy-based learns π(a|s, θ) directly by gradient ascent. Policy-based handles continuous actions and stochastic policies and changes smoothly, but has higher variance and finds local optima.

q: When can the optimal policy be stochastic?
short: Under partial observability/state aliasing (short corridor: identical-looking cells with reversed controls) and in adversarial games (rock–paper–scissors); in fully observed MDPs a deterministic optimum exists.

q: State the policy gradient theorem.
short: ∇J(θ) ∝ Σ_s μ(s) Σ_a q_π(s, a)∇π(a|s, θ) = E_π[q_π(S, A)∇ln π(A|S, θ)]; the gradient doesn't require differentiating the state distribution.

q: REINFORCE: θ = [0.5, −0.2], first action, G = 2, α = 0.1.
mistakes: Using π instead of one-hot − π.

q: Why does a baseline not bias the policy gradient?
short: E[b(S)∇ln π(A|S)] = Σ_s μ(s) b(s) Σ_a ∇π(a|s) = Σ_s μ(s) b(s) ∇1 = 0, as long as b doesn't depend on the action.

q: What is an actor–critic method?
short: An actor (policy) updated with an advantage estimate from a critic (value function); one-step version uses the TD error δ = R + γv̂(S′) − v̂(S) for both critic and actor updates.
mistakes: Calling REINFORCE with baseline actor–critic (no bootstrapping).

q: Why does a Gaussian policy suit continuous actions?
short: It outputs a mean and spread for each action dimension; sampling gives exploration, ∇ln π is analytic ((a − μ)/σ² for μ), and the mean converges toward good actions while σ adapts.

q: Derive the log-derivative trick.
short: ∇_θ E_{a~π}[f(a)] = Σ_a f(a)∇π(a) = Σ_a π(a) f(a) ∇ln π(a) = E_{a~π}[f(a)∇ln π(a)], using ∇π = π∇ln π.

q: REINFORCE with baseline vs actor–critic?
short: Both learn a value function, but REINFORCE with baseline uses it only to subtract from the Monte Carlo return (unbiased, high variance, end of episode); actor–critic bootstraps with it (biased, low variance, online).

q: What problem do natural gradients and TRPO solve?
short: Euclidean parameter steps can change the policy's behaviour unpredictably; natural gradients measure step size by KL divergence (Fisher metric), and TRPO enforces a KL trust region, giving monotonic-improvement guarantees in theory.
example: Collapsed policy after one large step.
mistakes: Thinking α tuning alone fixes it.

q: Explain PPO's clipped objective for negative advantages.
short: With A < 0 the objective wants r to fall. If r < 1 − ε, the clipped term (1 − ε)A is smaller than rA, so the min takes that constant: zero gradient, no further decrease. If r > 1 + ε, the unclipped rA is smaller and its gradient still pushes r down.
mistakes: Assuming symmetric clipping regardless of A.

q: What do A2C/A3C add to actor–critic?
short: Multiple parallel environment workers produce decorrelated experience (asynchronous updates in A3C, synchronised batches in A2C), often with n-step returns and an entropy bonus; this replaces replay for on-policy methods.

q: DDPG vs TD3 vs SAC?
short: DDPG: deterministic actor via ∇ₐQ, noise for exploration, prone to overestimation. TD3: twin critics with min, delayed actor updates, target smoothing. SAC: stochastic actor maximising reward + entropy with twin critics and auto-tuned temperature.

q: Why do policy gradient methods tend to be sample-inefficient?
short: Classic ones are on-policy: data must come from the current policy and is discarded after an update, and Monte Carlo-style estimates are noisy; PPO reuses a batch for a few epochs, off-policy actor–critics use replay.
follow: How does importance sampling help PPO?

q: Choose an algorithm for a real robot arm with expensive data.
short: Off-policy actor–critic (SAC or TD3) with replay for sample efficiency, safety limits on actions, pre-training in simulation with domain randomisation, then careful real-world fine-tuning; PPO if simulation is cheap and stability matters more.

q: How does the entropy bonus affect policy-gradient learning?
short: Adding βH(π(·|s)) to the objective penalises premature collapse to deterministic actions, keeping exploration alive and smoothing optimisation; too large β prevents committing to good actions.
detail: SAC makes it the objective itself.
mistakes: Thinking entropy bonus changes the optimum in the limit.

q: Why is PPO used for RLHF of language models?
short: Text generation is a sequence of discrete actions from a stochastic policy (the LM); PPO's clipped updates plus a KL penalty to the reference model keep changes stable and close to the pretrained behaviour while optimising a learned reward.

q: What is the optimal (variance-minimising) baseline intuition?
short: Roughly the return weighted by the squared score magnitude; in practice v̂(s) is a good, simple approximation because it centres returns around their expected value in each state.
follow: Does the baseline need to be accurate?

q: How does the gradient bandit (M2) relate to REINFORCE?
short: It is REINFORCE for a one-state problem: softmax preferences, update ∝ (R − R̄)(1{a = Aₜ} − π(a)), where R̄ is a baseline. Full policy gradients add states, returns and discounting.
